Project overview · updated 2026-10-19

Seafloor Physics World

A 3D ocean that opens in the browser, from barnacles on an intertidal rock to the floor of a trench 10,935 m down. Every scene is a real place built from measured data; light, currents and where animals live are worked out from physical and ecological rules wherever possible, and anything enlarged or simplified is said so on the page.

Approach

Find a real place first, then let physics draw it

The aim is to show the ocean as vast, strange and teeming with life, without painting it from imagination. Every new scene goes through the same process.

  1. Pick a real place and one phenomenon

    For example the coral reefs of the Paracel Islands, the octopus garden at the foot of Davidson Seamount, or the Arctic floe edge. The place needs published survey records, and the phenomenon has to explain one idea clearly: how light fades, how the tide sorts life into bands, how warm water shortens brooding.

  2. Read the sources and turn words into parameters

    Depth, temperature, water clarity, wave height and period, currents, sun angle, and the species, size, colour and density of the animals. The numbers come from papers, marine reserves, research institutes and encyclopaedias, all listed under Sources.

  3. Compute the picture with physical models

    One set of underwater optics, wave and ecology rules serves every scene: a new place is just new parameters. Where an animal appears is decided by its depth, temperature and habitat range, not placed by hand.

  4. Build the terrain and the animals

    Terrain, animal shapes and animation are all generated in code, with no external textures or model files, so the whole site is static and opens instantly.

  5. Check screenshots against photos

    Every scene is screenshotted in a browser and checked: do the colours look like real underwater photos, are the animals the right size, is anything unreadable or clipping through. If not, adjust and shoot again.

  6. Write the explanations, flag the simplifications

    Every feature has an explanation. Anything enlarged to be visible, simplified for speed, or estimated because no measurement was found is stated on the page.

  7. Narrate, test, publish

    The exhibition tour is voiced automatically on GitHub by MiniMax speech synthesis, in Chinese and English. Every push checks the build, that narration matches its audio, and that the docs are in sync, then publishes to GitHub Pages.

Real places

Every scene is a point on the map and can be found on the global relief map.

Compute rather than paint

The blue shift with depth, light shafts, sand ripples, bubble sizes and tide levels all come from formulas.

Say what is simplified

Estimates and simplifications (such as a 4 m tidal range) are stated on the page, not dressed up as precision.

Everything is explained

Welcome card, how-to, place introductions, field guide, info cards for every animal, and spoken narration.

Physical and ecological models

The formulas behind the picture

PhenomenonHow it is done
Underwater light and colourBeer–Lambert attenuation separately in red, green and blue, with coefficients set by water type; visibility, light shafts, Snell’s window, eye adaptation
TidesWhen following reality, an ocean model’s hourly forecast of sea level near Nanji (cubic interpolation); in fast-forward, a semidiurnal cosine with a 12.42 h period and range simplified to 4 m; the rocky shore moves with the tide level and barnacles put out their cirri only when submerged
Coral bleachingNOAA satellite heat stress (DHW) drives bleaching (noticeable from DHW 4, widespread from 8, some deaths from 12); branching corals most sensitive, massive most tolerant, upward sunlit surfaces first, fluorescent pigments fading with it
Waves and currentsLinear wave theory (dispersion relation) for wavelength and orbital velocity, a log-profile current; drives kelp sway, sand ripples and drift
Floe-edge lightingOnly about 3% of the light gets through the ice; nearer the edge and deeper down, more light spreads in sideways from the open water. Bubbles, camera and light shafts all use the same edge curve
Warm-spring refractionThe “shimmer” caused by the density difference of warm and cold water: spring positions are projected to the screen and a local ripple distortion is applied in post-processing
BubblesRise speed from water viscosity by temperature; expansion with depth by Boyle’s law
PressureHydrostatic pressure; the foam cup shrinks by a collapsing-cell model; water compressibility 4.6×10⁻¹⁰ /Pa
Deep sound channelMackenzie (1981) sound-speed equation with a measured temperature profile; 25 rays traced by Snell’s law
Daily vertical migrationAnimals follow an isolume of fixed brightness up and down, with limited swimming speed
Brine poolInternal waves on the interface between two liquids (reduced gravity g′ ≈ 0.30 m/s²), Fresnel reflection
Blue hole layersDissolved oxygen, hydrogen sulfide and cloudy layer at measured depths
BioluminescenceFlashes triggered only when flow shear stress exceeds about 0.15 Pa
Free pilotingThrust, quadratic drag, drift with currents and waves, 60 m tether
Global reliefNOAA ETOPO 20-arc-minute data, bilinearly interpolated for the relief map and profiles
Where animals liveEach species has a depth, temperature and habitat range; each scene decides who appears from these

The ocean today

What changes every day with the real world

The repository downloads real-world ocean data twice a day. The water temperature and bleaching of three coral reefs and the tide at the Nanji Islands follow reality, and the Arctic and Antarctic show today’s sea-ice extent. The animals are still simulated; what changes is the conditions they live in. The table shows the latest download.

PlaceTodaySource
Reading data/live.json…

How to watch: open the 3D world and press “How to watch” in the console’s “The ocean today” section. It explains the bleaching threshold, heat stress (DHW) and the alert levels, gives step-by-step things to look for and when to come back, and the limits of each kind of data.

Architecture

A static website plus two automated pipelines

3D scene

three.js r128 · WebGL

A hand-written shader patch, waterify(), gives every material underwater optics: separate red, green and blue attenuation, a scattering background, torch cones, caustics and sand ripples.

Source

src/ · 47 files

Split by feature (optics, seafloor, fish schools, each place, interface, tour…) and joined by tools/build.py into the js/seafloor.js the page loads. Only Python is needed.

Post-processing

render → bloom → white balance

Half-float rendering; bloom gives bioluminescence its glow; then white balance, vignette, torch halo and the heat shimmer above warm springs. Smooth mode turns bloom off.

Narration

narration/*.json → MiniMax

When the script changes, GitHub Actions calls MiniMax speech synthesis for both languages and commits the mp3 files. The key lives only in the repository’s encrypted secrets; the page just plays the finished audio.

Bilingual

src/00-i18n.js · i18n/en.json

Chinese is the source text. In English mode each string is looked up in a 1,000-plus entry dictionary; tools/i18n.py lists anything untranslated, and the checks fail if a string is missing.

Checks and publishing

check.py · smoke_test.py · GitHub Pages

Every push checks the build, syntax, narration-audio pairing and docs. Locally a headless browser runs the scenes, tour, map, postcards, VR and piloting in both languages. The repository root is served as the site.

src/*.js ──build.py──▶ js/seafloor.js ──▶ index.html ──▶ GitHub Pages narration/tour.json, tour.en.json ──GitHub Actions + MiniMax──▶ audio/tour/(en/)*.mp3 update log in index.html ──sync_docs.py──▶ docs/CHANGELOG.md · ROADMAP.md · SOURCES.md · overview(.en).html

Open issues

What isn’t done yet, or can’t be done in code

Each item says why, and what solving it would take. Those marked “needs you” can’t be finished by writing code alone.

needs you

Real ocean recordings

Sound is currently synthesised with Web Audio: surf, breathing and bubbles, sperm whale clicks, the hum of the deep. Real recordings (whale song, the crackle of a reef, seals under the ice) would add a lot, but recordings are copyrighted and can’t simply be downloaded.

recordings we are allowed to use (your own, or ones clearly licensed for reuse with attribution, such as some NOAA and MBARI public acoustic data). The editing, mixing by place and depth, and credits can then be done here.

needs devices

Testing on phones, gyroscopes and VR headsets

All tests run in a headless desktop browser. Smooth mode and automatic switching on stutter are in place, but performance on different phones, gyroscope orientation and WebXR headsets need trying on real hardware.

open the site on your phone (and a VR headset if you have one) and report anything that stutters or is confusing.

visuals

Animals are still simplified, code-built shapes

To run smoothly on phones without external files, animals are assembled from geometry, with no textures or skeletal animation, so they read as models. Octopuses and Sargassum look somewhat cartoonish.

for more realism, rigged glTF models: suitably licensed models (or commissioned ones), and accepting a heavier page.

data

Some values are estimates

The water depth at the Arctic floe edge is taken as about 300 m and the Nanji tidal range is simplified to 4 m, as no measurements were found; the global relief grid is about 37 km, so the trench shows only about 9,000 m deep on the map. All of this is noted on the page.

local measured data (tide tables, soundings) to replace the estimates.

models

The physics is simplified, not a numerical simulation

Schools use flocking rules, currents and waves use analytic formulas, and optics uses only three colour bands; there is no real fluid dynamics or radiative transfer. Fine for showing and teaching, not for research.

nothing for now; any single phenomenon can be made more precise on its own (for example measured spectra instead of three bands).

review

Content has not been reviewed by ocean scientists

All text was checked against published sources, but no specialist has gone through it line by line. The English is machine-assisted and hand-checked, and may read awkwardly in places.

for classroom or exhibition use, a marine biologist or physical oceanographer looking over the field guide and place texts; a native English reader flagging clumsy sentences.

accessibility

Not yet tried by an actual screen-reader user

The text description (G key) lists the current place, the readings and the animals you can see nearby, with each one’s direction from your line of sight and its distance; once the view has focus, the arrow keys turn it and +/− zoom, and the panels and tour work with a keyboard. All of this has only been checked by automated tests.

someone who uses a screen reader (VoiceOver, NVDA) trying it and telling us what reads badly or is missing.

What next

Where this could go

New places and phenomena

  • Great Barrier Reef bleaching · a timeline driven by water temperature, before and after
  • Sargasso Sea · a floating forest of seaweed in mid-ocean and its residents
  • Lost City vent field · white carbonate chimneys, set against black smokers
  • Humpback whale song · sound travelling along the deep sound channel, tied to the existing channel experiment
  • Submarine canyons and turbidity currents · sediment avalanching down a canyon
  • Dugongs of the northern South China Sea · historical records to explain “functional extinction”

Live data

  • Done · NOAA coral heat stress, the Nanji tide, Arctic and Antarctic sea ice: see “Live data”
  • Argo floats · measured temperature and salinity profiles driving the dive
  • Waves and sea temperature · from the same marine API, today’s swell for the kelp forest and water temperature everywhere
  • Local day and night · each place’s local time deciding day or night and the sun’s height

Experience and teaching

  • More languages · the language-pack structure is in place; a new one needs only a translation
  • Classroom mode · a teacher picks places and questions, students answer as they watch
  • Video export · record the tour straight to a video for sharing
  • Longer narration per place · from one clip to three: what to see, how it works, why it matters
  • A soundscape from real recordings · see open issues

Sources

73 sources

The places, parameters and species information on the page draw on these sources, newest first. Filter by keyword, for example “coral”, “NOAA” or “ice”.

  1. NOAA Coral Reef Watch: daily SST, HotSpot, DHW and bleaching alerts from 5 km regional virtual stations (Paracels, Hainan, Gulf of Aqaba)
  2. EcoWatch (2024): NOAA Coral Reef Watch adds bleaching Alert Levels 3–5 (DHW 12, 16, 20)
  3. Mongabay (2025): even the Gulf of Aqaba’s “supercorals” bleached in the 2024 heatwave
  4. Open-Meteo marine API: hourly sea level including tides from the Météo-France SMOC model
  5. NSIDC Sea Ice Index v4: daily sea-ice extent and the 1981–2010 climatology
  6. Ramsar information sheet: Nanji Islands, 19,893 ha, 422 algae and 725 shellfish and other molluscs, joined Man and the Biosphere in 1998
  7. Journal of Shanghai Ocean University (2017): 125 macrobenthic species in the Nanji intertidal, dominated by Tetraclita barnacles, thick-shelled mussels, Septifer mussels and periwinkles
  8. Frontiers in Marine Science (2025): Sargassum thunbergii dominates the brown algae of the upper shore; the upper subtidal is almost all Sargassum
  9. Davidson Seamount: 42 km long, about 2,280 m high, summit 1,250 m deep, 237 species
  10. AAAS (Barry et al., Science Advances 2023): 5,718 octopuses, springs up to 10.8 °C, brooding about 1.8 years, the “shimmer” in the water
  11. CNN: the octopus garden at about 3,200 m, found in 2018, may hold up to twenty thousand
  12. Arctic Kingdom: what the floe edge is; narwhals and belugas along the edge from late May to late June, ice about 2 m thick
  13. Ice algae: live on the ice underside and in brine channels, photosynthesising in as little as about 0.02% of surface light; Melosira strands can reach 1 m
  14. Alfred Wegener Institute (Kohlbach et al.): 50–90% of the carbon in young polar cod comes from ice algae, mostly via under-ice amphipods
  15. Boetius et al. (Science, 2013): Melosira made up 45% of central Arctic primary production in 2012 and sank to the deep sea in clumps as the ice melted
  16. WWF Canada: narwhal tusks and dive depths; about three quarters of the world’s narwhals are in Canada
  17. NOAA Fisheries: beluga length, dark-grey calves, unfused neck vertebrae, “canaries of the sea”
  18. NASA Earth Observatory: the 2025 Arctic sea-ice minimum, about 4.6 million km², tied with 2008 as the 10th lowest
  19. Biodiversity Science (2024): seagrass species across Hainan; Thalassia and Enhalus at Xincun
  20. Ministry of Ecology and Environment: restoring Xincun Bay, Lingshui, and China’s first special seagrass protection area
  21. Xinhua (2025): the Xincun lagoon mangrove wetland park, Lingshui
  22. Enhalus: leaves 30–150 cm long, male flowers float to the surface to pollinate
  23. UN Environment Programme: seagrass covers about 0.2% of the seafloor and stores about 10% of ocean carbon
  24. Functional extinction of the dugong in China (Lin, Turvey et al., 2022)
  25. Upside-down jellyfish: photosynthesis by symbiotic algae
  26. The Paper: species records in the Dongzhaigang mangrove reserve
  27. Bonifácio et al. (2021): extent and depth of the Clarion-Clipperton Zone
  28. World Ocean Review: formation, size, growth rate and abundance of manganese nodules
  29. Rabone et al. (2023): 5,578 animal species recorded in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, about 90% undescribed
  30. Jones et al. (2025, Nature): the 1979 mining-test track 44 years on
  31. Purser et al. (2016): ghost octopuses laying eggs on the stalks of sponges on nodules
  32. Depth range and habits of the tripod fish (Bathypterois grallator)
  33. Dodgson (2004): distribution of human interpupillary distance (adult mean about 63 mm)
  34. MDN: WebXR Device API
  35. NOAA: ETOPO global relief model
  36. basemap sample data (ETOPO 20 arc-minutes)
  37. NOAA Ocean Explorer: foam cups taken to 2,500 m

  40. DOSITS: discovery and uses of the deep sound channel
  41. Sound speed profile (Wikipedia)
  42. Latz: the fluid-shear threshold for dinoflagellate bioluminescence
